newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK dollar at two-year low, but raising few fears.
newsitem.headline: HK dollar at two-year low, but raising few fears.

text.p: The Hong Kong dollar was mired at two-year lows against the U.S. dollar on Wednesday, but analysts said there was little cause for concern as the slump was partly linked to seasonal factors and was losing momentum.
Hong Kong's dollar was stuck at 7.7496/06 to the U.S. unit on Wednesday, its weakest level since January 1995 following the Mexican peso crisis when it dropped to around HK$7.77.
The rate is pegged at HK$7.8 to the dollar but has tended to trade between HK$7.73 and HK$7.74 for the past few years.
The T.T. -- or telegraphic transfer, as the U.S. dollar-Hong Kong dollar exchange rate is called -- started to rise around January 20 and soared above 7.74 on January 23.

Analysts attributed its strength to keen demand for the U.S. dollar from corporate players, funds switching out of local stocks to other regional bourses, and note-issuing banks ahead of the Chinese New Year holidays which start on Thursday.
"(Note-issuing) banks print notes ahead of Chinese New Year every year," said Standard Chartered Bank treasurer Stanley Wong. "The banks need to buy U.S. dollars from the market."
Hong Kong's three note-issuing banks must have U.S. dollars on hand before they issue the equivalent in local dollar notes.

There is usually a surge in demand for bank notes ahead of Chinese New Year when people withdraw more than normal amounts of cash to buy goods and gifts for the festival and to give traditional envelopes of "lucky money".
Chase Manhattan Bank foreign exchange manager Tony Cheung said the local unit lost ground as some fund managers switched out of the Hong Kong stock market.
"Some funds are flowing out of Hong Kong stocks into other regional markets," Cheung said.
Wong said the T.T. did not rise as notably this time last year when only the Chinese New Year factor was in play.
"Some corporate players started to buy the U.S. dollar in greater amounts at a T.T. above 7.74 after they had waited in vain for the U.S. dollar to fall to lower levels," he said.

A banker at a regional institution said that with no visible intervention from the territory's de factor central bank, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), some traders were testing the authority to see where it might intervene.
That put further pressure on the Hong Kong dollar, he said.

"It seems that the HKMA is quite willing to let the Hong Kong dollar have a wider trading band. They seem to be quite comfortable with the Hong Kong dollar at 7.75 (and) willing to let the dollar float outside the 7.73 to 7.74 range," he said.
He saw the HKMA moves as a good policy since too rigid a band would make it more difficult for it to defend the local dollar in case of attack.
HKMA officials were not immediately available to comment.

The authority has frequently warned speculators against using any uncertainty ahead of Hong Kong's handover to China on July 1 as an opportunity to take a run at the local dollar, pointing to the territory's US$63.8 billion in foreign reserves.
Analysts and traders said the Hong Kong dollar's fall had decelerated this week compared to last week, and would gradually reverse course.
"The T.T. rise has slowed down in the past few days after rising quite a lot last Thursday and Friday," Wong said. "After the Chinese New Year, it will be back to 7.7450."
Chase Manhattan's Cheung said: "We think it will stand at 7.7490/00 for a while and then fall back."
-- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843 6590
